summary.text: A stationary distribution is a special distribution for a Markov chain: if the chain starts with it, the distribution over states stays the same at every later time.
If the chain is irreducible, the stationary distribution is always unique when it exists.
When the chain is irreducible and aperiodic, it can be read as the limiting distribution, and it relates to eigenvectors with eigenvalue one.

facts.label: Defining feature
facts.value: Starting in it keeps the state distribution the same at all times

facts.label: Uniqueness
facts.value: Unique if it exists, assuming irreducibility

facts.label: Limiting role
facts.value: The limiting distribution when the chain is irreducible and aperiodic

facts.label: Linear algebra link
facts.value: Related to eigenvectors with eigenvalue one

facts.label: Other name
facts.value: Called a stable distribution in some fields

items.prompt: A chain starts with its stationary distribution. What does the spread of states look like at time 10, or at time 1,000?

options.label: It grows more uneven over time
It is the same stationary distribution
It resets to a different starting guess
It cycles through a new distribution each step

items.explain: If the chain starts with its stationary distribution, the distribution of states at any later time will always be that same distribution.

items.prompt: A Markov chain is irreducible. How many stationary distributions can it have?

options.label: One for every possible starting state
Exactly two
At most one
Infinitely many

items.explain: Assuming irreducibility, the stationary distribution is always unique if it exists.

items.prompt: A chain is both irreducible and aperiodic. After a very long time, what does its distribution over states approach?

options.label: Its starting distribution
An even split with nothing special about it
A distribution that changes forever
Its stationary distribution

items.explain: For an irreducible and aperiodic chain, the stationary distribution can be interpreted as the limiting distribution.

items.prompt: In linear algebra terms, a stationary distribution is closely related to which kind of vector?

options.label: An eigenvector whose eigenvalue is one
A vector that sums to zero
An eigenvector whose eigenvalue is zero
A vector of all zeros

items.explain: Stationary distributions are related to eigenvectors for which the eigenvalue is unity.

items.prompt: In general, for something that a matrix or operator leaves unchanged, must there be only one such thing?

options.label: Yes, there can be only one in every case
Yes, but only when the matrix is square
No, it need not be unique
No, there are always at least three

items.explain: A stationary distribution is an entity unchanged by an operator, and in the general concept it need not be unique.

items.prompt: An engineer calls a chain's unchanging distribution a stable distribution, but a statistician hears something else. Why the mismatch?

options.label: The engineer is describing a different kind of chain
Statisticians never use the word stable
The two are the same thing under another spelling
In probability and statistics that term has a rather different meaning

items.explain: Some fields use stable distribution for the stationary distribution, but in probability and statistics the term has a rather different meaning.
